danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Den ottende september trådte en officer — en meget fornem at dømme efter den respekt, vagten viste ham — ind i vognskuret, hvor fangerne sad. Denne officer, formodentlig en stabsofficer, holdt et papir i hånden og kaldte alle russerne op, idet han omtalte Pierre som »manden, der ikke opgiver sit navn«. Med et sløvt og ligegyldigt blik på alle fangerne beordrede han den vagthavende officer til at sørge for, at de blev ordentligt klædt og gjort præsentable, inden de blev bragt for marskalken. En time senere ankom en deling soldater, og Pierre blev med tretten andre ført til Jomfru-Marken. Det var en smuk dag, solrig efter regn, og luften var usædvanligt ren. Røgen hang ikke lavt som den dag, Pierre var hentet fra vagtposten ved Zúbovskij-volden, men steg i søjler gennem den rene luft. Ingen flammer var synlige, men røgsøjler steg fra alle sider, og hele Moskva, så langt Pierre kunne se, var én stor forkullet ruin. Overalt var der øde pladser, hvor kun kakkelovne og skorstenspiber endnu stod, og hist og her de sværtede vægge af murstenshuse. Pierre stirrede på ruinerne og genkendte ikke kvarterer, han havde kendt godt. Hist og her kunne han se kirker, der ikke var brændt. Kreml, der var uskadt, skinnede hvidt i det fjerne med sine tårne og Ivan den Stores klokketårn. Kuplerne på Det Nye Jomfrukloster glitrede klart, og dets klokker ringede særligt tydeligt. Disse klokker mindede Pierre om, at det var søndag og Marie Fødselsdag. Men der syntes ikke at være nogen til at fejre denne helligdag: overalt var der sværtede ruiner, og de få russere, man så, var pjaltede og forskræmte mennesker, der forsøgte at skjule sig, når de så franskmændene.

Det var tydeligt, at den russiske rede var ødelagt og tilintetgjort, men i stedet for den russiske livsorden, der var blevet ødelagt, følte Pierre ubevidst, at en ganske anden, fast, fransk orden var blevet oprettet over denne ødelagte rede. Han fornam det i blikkene fra de soldater, der i ordnede rækker, raske og muntre, ledsagede ham og de andre forbrydere; han fornam det i blikkene fra en vigtig fransk embedsmand i en hesteforspændt vogn, kørt af en soldat, som de mødte undervejs. Han fornam det i de muntre lyde af regimentsmusik, der hørtes fra feltets venstre side, og fornam og forstod det særligt af den liste over fanger, den franske officer havde læst op, da han kom den morgen. Pierre var taget af én gruppe soldater og ført først til ét og derefter til et andet sted med snesevis af andre mænd, og det syntes, som om de kunne have glemt ham eller forvekslet ham med de andre. Men nej: de svar, han havde givet ved afhøringen, var vendt tilbage til ham i hans betegnelse som »manden, der ikke opgiver sit navn«, og under den betegnelse, der for Pierre syntes frygtelig, blev han nu med urokkelig sikkerhed i deres ansigter ført et sted hen, i forvisningen om, at han og alle de andre fanger var nøjagtigt dem, de ville have, og at de blev ført til det rette sted. Pierre følte sig som en ubetydelig spån, der var faldet ind mellem hjulene i en maskine, hvis funktion han ikke forstod, men som fungerede godt.

Han og de andre fanger blev ført til højre side af Jomfru-Marken, til et stort hvidt hus med en uhyre have, ikke langt fra klostret. Det var fyrst Sjtjerbátovs hus, hvor Pierre ofte havde været i andre dage, og som nu, erfarede han af soldaternes snak, var optaget af marskalken, hertugen af Eckmühl (Davout).

De blev ført til indgangen og en efter en ind i huset. Pierre var den sjette. Han blev ført gennem et glasgalleri, et forværelse og en sal, der alle var ham velkendte, ind i et langt, lavloftet arbejdsværelse, ved hvis dør en adjudant stod.

Davout, med briller på næsen, sad foroverbøjet over et bord i den fjerne ende af værelset. Pierre gik helt hen til ham, men Davout, der tydeligvis konsulterede et papir foran sig, så ikke op. Uden at løfte øjnene sagde han med lav stemme:
»Hvem er De?«

Pierre tav, fordi han var ude af stand til at frembringe et ord. For ham var Davout ikke blot en fransk general, men en mand berygtet for sin grusomhed. Da Pierre betragtede hans kolde ansigt, mens han sad der som en streng skolelærer, der var indstillet på at vente et stykke tid på et svar, følte Pierre, at hvert sekunds tøven kunne koste ham livet; men han vidste ikke, hvad han skulle sige. Han turde ikke gentage, hvad han havde sagt ved den første afhøring, men at afsløre sin rang og stilling var farligt og pinligt. Så han tav. Men inden han havde besluttet sig, løftede Davout hovedet, skubbede brillerne op på panden, kneb øjnene sammen og så Pierre fast i øjnene.
»Jeg kender den mand,« sagde han i en kold, afmålt tone, der tydeligt var beregnet på at skræmme Pierre.
Den kulde, der havde løbet Pierre ned ad ryggen, greb nu hans hoved som i en skruestik.
»De kan umuligt kende mig, general, jeg har aldrig set Dem...«
»Han er en russisk spion,« afbrød Davout og henvendte sig til en anden general, der var til stede, men som Pierre ikke havde bemærket.
Davout vendte sig bort. Med et uventet genlyd i stemmen begyndte Pierre hastigt:
»Nej, monseigneur,« sagde han, idet han pludselig huskede, at Davout var hertug. »Nej, monseigneur, De kan ikke have kendt mig. Jeg er militsofficer og har ikke forladt Moskva.«
»Deres navn?« spurgte Davout.
»Bezukhov.«
»Hvilket bevis har jeg for, at De ikke lyver?«
»Monseigneur!« udbrød Pierre, ikke med en fornærmet men med en bønfaldende stemme.

Davout så op og stirrede fast på ham. I nogle sekunder så de på hinanden, og det blik reddede Pierre. Ud over krigens og lovens betingelser skabte det blik en menneskelig forbindelse mellem de to mænd. I det øjeblik gik et utal af ting dunkelt gennem begges sind, og de erkendte, at de begge var menneskehedens børn og var brødre.

Ved det første blik, da Davout kun havde løftet hovedet fra papirerne, hvor menneskelige anliggender og liv var angivet ved tal, var Pierre blot en omstændighed, og Davout kunne have ladet ham skyde uden at tynge sin samvittighed med en ond gerning, men nu så han et menneske i ham. Han betænkte sig et øjeblik.
»Hvordan kan De bevise mig, at De taler sandt?« sagde Davout koldt.
Pierre huskede Ramballe og nævnte ham og hans regiment og den gade, hvor huset lå.
»De er ikke, hvad De siger,« svarede Davout.
Med skælvende, famlende stemme begyndte Pierre at fremlægge beviser for sandheden af sine udsagn.
Men i det øjeblik trådte en adjudant ind og rapporterede noget til Davout.
Davout lysede op af den nyhed, adjudanten bragte, og begyndte at knappe sin uniform. Han syntes helt at have glemt Pierre.

Da adjudanten mindede ham om fangen, nikkede han med et rysten i Pierres retning med rynkede bryn og beordrede, at han skulle føres bort. Men hvorhen de skulle bringe ham, vidste Pierre ikke: tilbage til vognskuret eller til henrettelsespladsen, som hans medfanger havde peget ud for ham, da de krydsede Jomfru-Marken.
Han vendte hovedet og så, at adjudanten stillede Davout endnu et spørgsmål.
»Ja, selvfølgelig!« svarede Davout, men hvad dette »ja« betød, vidste Pierre ikke.

Pierre kunne bagefter ikke huske, hvordan han gik, om det var langt, eller i hvilken retning. Hans evner var fuldstændig lammet, han var bedøvet og lagde intet mærke til omkring sig, men blev ved med at bevæge benene, som de andre gjorde, indtil de alle standsede, og han standsede med. Den eneste tanke i hans sind var: hvem var det, der virkelig havde dømt ham til døden? Ikke mændene i kommissionen, der først havde afhørt ham — ikke én af dem ønskede det eller kunne åbenbart have gjort det. Det var ikke Davout, der havde set på ham på en så menneskelig måde. Et øjeblik endnu, og Davout ville have indset, at han handlede forkert, men netop da var adjudanten kommet ind og havde afbrudt ham. Adjudanten havde tydeligvis heller ikke haft onde hensigter, skønt han kunne have afholdt sig fra at komme ind. Hvem var det da, der henrettede ham, dræbte ham, berøvede ham livet — ham, Pierre, med alle hans minder, forhåbninger, håb og tanker? Hvem gjorde dette? Og Pierre følte, at det var ingen.
Det var et system — en sammenkædning af omstændigheder.
Et eller andet system dræbte ham — Pierre — berøvede ham livet, alt, tilintetgjorde ham.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: On the eighth of September an officer came into the coach house where the prisoners were held. Judging by the respect the guards showed him, he was a very important one, probably someone on the staff. He held a paper in his hand and called over all the Russians there, naming Pierre as "the man who does not give his name." He glanced lazily and indifferently at all the prisoners, then ordered the officer in charge to have them decently dressed and tidied before taking them to the marshal. An hour later a squad of soldiers arrived, and Pierre and thirteen others were led to the Virgin's Field. It was a fine day, sunny after rain, and the air was unusually clear. The smoke didn't hang low, as on the day Pierre had been taken from the guardhouse on the Zubovski rampart, but rose through the clear air in columns. No flames were visible, but columns of smoke rose on every side, and all Moscow, as far as Pierre could see, was one vast charred ruin. Everywhere there were empty spaces with only stoves and chimney stacks left standing, and here and there the blackened walls of some brick houses. Pierre gazed at the ruins and did not recognize districts he had known well. Here and there he could see churches that hadn't burned. The Kremlin, which was not destroyed, gleamed white in the distance with its towers and the belfry of Ivan the Great. The domes of the New Convent of the Virgin glittered brightly and its bells were ringing particularly clearly. These bells reminded Pierre that it was Sunday and the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin. But there seemed to be no one to celebrate the holiday. Everywhere were blackened ruins, and the few Russians to be seen were tattered, frightened people who tried to hide when they saw the French.

The Russian nest was plainly ruined and destroyed. But Pierre sensed without quite knowing it that over this ruined nest a quite different, firm, French order had been set up in place of the Russian way of life. He felt it in the looks of the soldiers who were escorting him and the other criminals, marching in regular ranks, brisk and cheerful. He felt it in the look of an important French official in a carriage and pair, driven by a soldier, whom they met on the way. He felt it in the merry sounds of regimental music from the left side of the field, and he felt and understood it especially from the list of prisoners the French officer had read out that morning. One set of soldiers had taken Pierre and led him first to one place and then to another with dozens of other men, and it seemed they might have forgotten him or mixed him up with the others. But no: the answers he had given when questioned had come back to him in the label "the man who does not give his name." Under that name, which seemed terrible to Pierre, they were now leading him somewhere, with the unhesitating assurance on their faces that he and all the other prisoners were exactly the ones they wanted and were being taken to the right place. Pierre felt like an insignificant chip fallen among the wheels of a machine whose workings he didn't understand but which was running well.

He and the other prisoners were taken to the right side of the Virgin's Field, to a large white house with an immense garden, not far from the convent. This was Prince Shcherbatov's house, where Pierre had often been in other days. From the soldiers' talk he learned that the marshal, the Duke of Eckmühl (Davout), now occupied it.

They were taken to the entrance and led into the house one at a time. Pierre was the sixth to go in. He was taken through a glass gallery, an anteroom and a hall, all familiar to him, into a long low study, with an adjutant standing at the door.

Davout sat bent over a table at the far end of the room, with spectacles on his nose. Pierre went right up to him, but Davout, evidently reading a paper in front of him, did not look up. Without raising his eyes, he said in a low voice:
"Who are you?"

Pierre was silent because he couldn't utter a word. To him Davout was not merely a French general but a man notorious for his cruelty. He looked at that cold face, at the man sitting like a stern schoolmaster ready to wait a while for an answer, and felt that every moment's delay might cost him his life. But he didn't know what to say. He didn't dare repeat what he had said at his first examination, yet revealing his rank and position was dangerous and embarrassing. So he stayed silent. But before he had decided what to do, Davout raised his head, pushed his spectacles back onto his forehead, screwed up his eyes and looked at him intently.
"I know that man," he said in a cold, measured tone, evidently meant to frighten Pierre.
The chill that had been running down Pierre's back now gripped his head like a vise.
"You can't know me, General, I have never seen you..."
"He is a Russian spy," Davout interrupted, speaking to another general who was in the room, though Pierre hadn't noticed him.
Davout turned away. With an unexpected ring in his voice, Pierre began quickly:
"No, monseigneur," he said, suddenly remembering that Davout was a duke. "No, monseigneur, you can't have known me. I'm a militia officer and I haven't left Moscow."
"Your name?" asked Davout.
"Bezukhov."
"What proof have I that you are not lying?"
"Monseigneur!" exclaimed Pierre, not offended but pleading.

Davout looked up and gazed at him intently. For a few seconds they looked at each other, and that look saved Pierre. Quite apart from the conditions of war and law, that look set up a human relationship between the two men. In that moment a vast number of things passed dimly through both their minds, and they realized that they were both children of humanity and were brothers.

At the first glance, when Davout had only raised his head from the papers where human affairs and lives were shown as numbers, Pierre was merely a circumstance, and Davout could have shot him without burdening his conscience with an evil deed. But now he saw a human being in him. He thought for a moment.
"How can you show me that you are telling the truth?" said Davout coldly.
Pierre remembered Ramballe, and named him, his regiment and the street where the house was.
"You are not what you say," Davout answered.
In a trembling, faltering voice Pierre began to offer proofs that his statements were true.
But at that moment an adjutant came in and reported something to Davout.
Davout brightened at the news the adjutant brought and began buttoning up his uniform. He seemed to have forgotten Pierre completely.

When the adjutant reminded him of the prisoner, he jerked his head toward Pierre with a frown and ordered him taken away. But where they were to take him Pierre didn't know: back to the coach house, or to the place of execution his companions had pointed out as they crossed the Virgin's Field.
He turned his head and saw the adjutant putting another question to Davout.
"Yes, of course!" replied Davout, but what this "yes" meant, Pierre didn't know.

Pierre couldn't remember afterward how he walked, whether it was far, or in which direction. His faculties were numbed, he was stupefied, and he noticed nothing around him. He kept moving his legs as the others did until they all stopped and he stopped too. The only thought in his mind at that time was: who was it that had really sentenced him to death? Not the men on the commission that had first examined him: not one of them wished to do it or, evidently, could have. It wasn't Davout, who had looked at him in so human a way. In another moment Davout would have realized he was doing wrong, but just then the adjutant had come in and interrupted him. The adjutant, too, evidently had no evil intent, though he might have stayed out. Then who was executing him, killing him, taking his life, him, Pierre, with all his memories, aspirations, hopes and thoughts? Who was doing this? And Pierre felt that it was no one.
It was a system, a coming together of circumstances.
A system of some sort was killing him, Pierre, taking his life and everything else, wiping him out.
